question: Can a conditional diffusion model trained on millions of saved optimization trajectories act as a useful learned optimizer for unseen neural-network initializations, and do one-update performance, prompt control, multimodality, scaling, and nearest-neighbor evidence establish efficient optimization and genuine weight-space generalization?

key_findings.claim: G.pt learns a conditional distribution over a later checkpoint, not a general update rule: it receives an earlier parameter vector and metric plus a desired future metric, then denoises a later parameter vector sampled from the same stored training run.
key_findings.evidence: Training first samples a run uniformly, samples an ordered pair of checkpoints from that run, noises the later parameters, and minimizes signal-prediction MSE. Separate models are trained for each architecture, task, and conditioning metric, so the method primarily imitates fixed training-trajectory distributions rather than learning an architecture- or task-agnostic optimizer.

key_findings.claim: The parameter-space diffusion transformer is technically coherent for the small fixed architectures studied.
key_findings.evidence: Weights and biases are flattened into layer tokens, oversized layers are chunked below a maximum token width, scalar metrics and diffusion time use frequency encodings, and a bidirectional GPT-2-style transformer maps uniquely encoded tokens back through per-token decoders. A global residual from the starting network changes the target to a parameter update and enables identity initialization.

key_findings.claim: The headline 'one-step' comparison is not compute-matched: one G.pt update executes a 1,000-step reverse diffusion chain, whereas each SGD or Adam comparator receives one literal gradient update.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 3 and 4 frame one generated parameter sample as one update and compare it with one gradient step. Table 1 fixes J=1000 for every G.pt model, and the released sampler iterates the full DDPM chain. The paper reports neither inference wall time nor FLOPs, so the experiment establishes outer-update compression, not faster optimization.

key_findings.claim: Within that asymmetric one-update protocol, G.pt produces much better task metrics than a single tuned SGD, momentum, NAG, RMSprop, or Adam update on five unseen random initializations.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 reports a Cartpole return near 450 versus near-zero to small baseline returns, MNIST test loss near 0.2 versus roughly 2.1-2.3, and CIFAR-10 test error near 50% versus roughly 90%. The baselines use a 3-by-3 learning-rate and weight-decay grid, but prompt values can be placed slightly above or below the dataset best when that works better and only five seeds support the error bars.

key_findings.claim: G.pt controls achieved return, loss, and error across much of the observed prompt range, but it underfits CIFAR-10 and does not reliably extrapolate beyond metrics represented in its checkpoint corpus.
key_findings.evidence: Desired-versus-observed plots over 20 prompts show strong average alignment for Cartpole and MNIST and visibly noisier or biased CIFAR-10 responses. The authors explicitly limit the claim to values represented by the pre-training data and list loss-landscape underfitting and poor prompt extrapolation as limitations.

key_findings.claim: Prompt-alignment scaling improves sharply with model and data size in the tested range, but remains unsaturated and is selected using the best evaluation score observed over training.
key_findings.evidence: Six G.pt sizes span roughly 2M to 858M parameters; models below about 60M fail and the 858M endpoint remains on a rising curve. For the 858M model, increasing the corpus from 500 to 25,000 runs (100K to 5M checkpoints) improves alignment, while 25,000 to 55,000 runs gives little additional gain. Each plotted model checkpoint is the one attaining the highest prompt alignment over training, and the metric averages R-squared across only 128 unseen networks and 20 prompts.

key_findings.claim: Recursive prompting helps substantially on unseen initialization distributions, but the evidence is confined to the same MNIST MLP architecture and task.
key_findings.evidence: Across Xavier normal/uniform, orthogonal, and Kaiming fan-in/fan-out variants absent from checkpoint generation, up to ten recursive low-error prompts reduce test error. The in-distribution case converges in about one update; several shifted distributions require multiple updates and retain different residual errors.

key_findings.claim: Permutation augmentation and dense intermediate trajectories are important to the reported generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Removing function-preserving neuron permutations drives Cartpole test prompt alignment near failure despite improving training fit. Replacing 200 checkpoints per run with only initial/final pairs worsens MNIST one-step test loss at a zero-loss prompt from about 0.20 to 0.32, more than 50%.

key_findings.claim: The paper shows stochastic and input-conditioned diversity, but its PCA surfaces do not establish a faithful multimodal distribution over functionally distinct optima.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 8 and 12 project 256 samples into sample-fitted top-two PCA directions and display only samples whose two-dimensional reconstruction error is below 10^-3. Appendix A further finds that resampling the starting initialization changes outputs more than resampling reverse-process noise. These selected two-dimensional views and first-layer images demonstrate variation, not mode coverage, probability calibration, or distinct behavior.

key_findings.claim: Supervised G.pt uses the benchmark test labels as dense meta-training supervision, so its reported CIFAR-10 and MNIST 'test' optimization is transductive rather than clean held-out evaluation.
key_findings.evidence: Every saved supervised checkpoint includes full test loss and error, and the loss- and error-conditional models train directly on those metrics. CIFAR-10.1 preserves a trend in which lower CIFAR-10-loss prompts lower shifted-set loss, but absolute loss degrades from 1.07 on CIFAR-10 to 1.51 on CIFAR-10.1 for the best stored checkpoint. This does not remove repeated access to the original test labels or provide an untouched iid test set.

key_findings.claim: The original nearest-neighbor score does not rule out memorization, and a later dedicated primary audit directly contradicts the paper's broad generalization interpretation.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix E counts whether a generated sample is closer to any of 200 checkpoints on the same held-out trajectory as its conditioning initialization than to millions of training checkpoints. That privileged trajectory comparison is not a novelty test and ignores symmetry-aligned nearest neighbors and simple interpolation baselines. Zeng et al. (CVPR 2026, arXiv:2506.07998) re-evaluated G.pt with permutation enumeration and behavior comparisons: the original 2.1M-checkpoint model had mean generated-to-training distance 2.25 versus 3.64 among training checkpoints and a ZU copying score of -8.5. Scaling to 20.4M checkpoints raised the score to 3.5 without lowering accuracy, showing that the original model's evidence was consistent with substantial copying.

key_findings.claim: The released artifact makes the core model and data available but does not fully reproduce the paper's empirical record.
key_findings.evidence: The official repository supplies code, five configs and pre-trained models, three checkpoint corpora, and a pinned Python 3.8/PyTorch 1.11 environment. The live archives total about 349 GB compressed and the model files about 32.3 GB, but the downloader provides no checksums, the repository has no tests or CI, and scripts for baseline tuning, model/data scaling, CIFAR-10.1, PCA surfaces, and the Appendix E memorization analysis are absent. The appendix checklist says total compute and hardware are reported, yet neither the paper source nor artifact states them.

method.core_idea: Treat saved neural-network parameters and their measured performance as a new training modality, then learn a conditional generative map from an earlier checkpoint and desired future metric to a later checkpoint.
method.mechanism: For each fixed task-level architecture, standard SGD, Adam, or PPO runs contribute 200 ordered checkpoints and metadata. Training uniformly samples a run and an earlier/later checkpoint pair, applies the same random hidden-unit permutation to both parameter vectors, normalizes parameters, noises the later vector at a random diffusion time, and trains an x0-predicting transformer with squared error. Weight and bias tensors become unique layer or chunk tokens; starting and target metrics and diffusion time become frequency tokens. A noncausal GPT-2-like transformer plus per-token decoders predicts the future parameters, with a global residual from the starting network. Inference begins from Gaussian noise and runs 1,000 DDPM denoising steps conditioned on the starting parameters and requested loss, error, or return.
assumptions: Trajectories produced by fixed conventional optimizers contain a reusable conditional law for future parameters.
A model trained on same-run checkpoint pairs will generalize beyond memorizing or interpolating stored trajectories.
Function-preserving neuron permutations are sufficient treatment of the major symmetries in weight space.
Raw Euclidean parameter distance remains meaningful after augmentation and across optimizer trajectories.
One task, architecture, and metric per G.pt model is an informative step toward a learned optimizer.
A 1,000-evaluation diffusion sample can be compared to one gradient update using update count rather than compute.
The requested metric lies inside the pre-training distribution and is adequately represented by a scalar frequency encoding.
Conditioning on benchmark test losses and errors does not invalidate claims about test performance.
Selecting the model checkpoint and one-step prompt by achieved prompt alignment or performance does not materially bias evaluation.
Twenty prompts, 128 networks, and five-seed optimizer bars adequately characterize reliability and tails.
Two-dimensional PCA projections with a reconstruction filter preserve the relevant mode structure.
Closeness to a held-out trajectory paired with the input initialization distinguishes generalization from memorization.
The cost of generating 100K-plus runs and training 347M-639M reported models is amortizable for target networks with only 1,250-7,960 parameters.

techniques.role: Builds a 23M-example parameter-and-metric corpus from more than 100K optimization runs.
Forms conditional training examples from ordered earlier and later checkpoints in one trajectory.
Applies matched hidden-unit permutations to input and target networks while preserving their functions.
Rescales the marginal parameter variance to match the image-domain range used to tune diffusion schedules.
Predicts clean future parameters rather than diffusion noise under a fixed 1,000-step linear schedule.
Serializes each weight or bias group as a token and chunks large tensors below a maximum width.
Encodes starting metric, requested metric, and diffusion time using sinusoidal frequency features.
Uses separate linear encoders and decoders for every parameter-token position.
Adds the starting network to the decoded output so G.pt learns an update and begins as identity.
Conditions generation on desired loss, classification error, or return, including nondifferentiable objectives.
Feeds generated parameters back as input for repeated test-time optimization.
Scores desired-versus-observed control with mean per-network R-squared over a prompt grid.
Projects generated MNIST parameters into two PCA directions and evaluates a local test-error surface.
Compares each sample with its input-linked held-out trajectory and the training corpus in Euclidean space.

evaluations.setting: One generated update from random initialization on Cartpole, MNIST, and CIFAR-10 across return, test-loss, and test-error conditioning
evaluations.metric: Achieved task metric over five initializations
evaluations.result: G.pt strongly outperforms one tuned update from every listed hand-designed optimizer and can directly condition on nondifferentiable return or classification error.
evaluations.baseline: One literal SGD, momentum, NAG, RMSprop, or Adam update; not matched to G.pt's 1,000 transformer evaluations, pre-training compute, or stored-run corpus.

evaluations.setting: Full gradient-training curves on the three headline tasks
evaluations.metric: Return, loss, or error versus optimizer update count
evaluations.result: One G.pt outer update reaches performance requiring hundreds to thousands of conventional updates in the displayed curves, but tuned multi-step gradient methods eventually match or supersede it.
evaluations.baseline: SGD and Adam curves over five initializations, without wall-clock, FLOP, or energy normalization.

evaluations.setting: Desired-versus-observed prompting from unseen initial parameters
evaluations.metric: Achieved return, MNIST loss, or CIFAR-10 error across 20 prompts
evaluations.result: Cartpole and MNIST responses broadly track prompts; CIFAR-10 is noisier and the method has limited out-of-range extrapolation.
evaluations.baseline: Identity line and the best metric represented in the training split; no calibrated conditional density or simple trajectory-regression baseline.

evaluations.setting: MNIST MLPs initialized with seven distributions absent from checkpoint generation
evaluations.metric: Test error over up to ten recursive G.pt updates
evaluations.result: Repeated prompting rapidly reduces error for Xavier, orthogonal, and Kaiming variants, though several shifts need multiple updates and converge less well than the in-distribution initialization.
evaluations.baseline: The paper's in-distribution initialization; no gradient optimizer, broader task shift, or architecture shift in this experiment.

evaluations.setting: Scaling six G.pt sizes from roughly 2M to 858M parameters
evaluations.metric: Mean prompt-alignment R-squared over 128 unseen networks and 20 prompts
evaluations.result: Models below about 60M fail, larger models improve sharply, and performance remains unsaturated at 858M.
evaluations.baseline: Randomly initialized G.pt near -2.7, with the best prompt-alignment checkpoint selected over training.

evaluations.setting: Scaling the 858M model from 500 to 55,000 runs, each with 200 checkpoints
evaluations.result: Performance improves strongly from 100K to 5M checkpoints and changes little from 5M to roughly 10M checkpoints.
evaluations.baseline: Smaller subsets of the same MNIST checkpoint distribution; no equal-compute or diverse-task comparison.

evaluations.setting: Fixed-input MNIST sampling and random-initialization resampling
evaluations.metric: PCA-local error surfaces, first-layer visualizations, and per-parameter variance over 4,096 DDIM samples
evaluations.result: Outputs vary with reverse noise and more strongly with the starting initialization; selected samples occupy multiple low-error regions in two-dimensional PCA plots.
evaluations.baseline: Ground-truth optimized first-layer weights and the two variance sources; no permutation-aligned functional diversity or coverage metric.

evaluations.metric: Cartpole train/test diffusion loss and prompt alignment; MNIST one-step test loss
evaluations.result: Permutation augmentation prevents severe test prompt-alignment failure, and using 200 intermediate checkpoints per run improves one-step loss from 0.32 to 0.20 versus initial/final pairs.
evaluations.baseline: No permutation augmentation and two checkpoints per run.

evaluations.metric: CIFAR-10.1 loss versus the CIFAR-10 loss prompt
evaluations.result: Lower CIFAR-10 prompts correlate with lower shifted-set loss, but generated models perform worse on CIFAR-10.1 and the best stored checkpoint changes from 1.07 to 1.51 loss.
evaluations.baseline: CIFAR-10 achieved loss and best checkpoint; no untouched iid holdout because original test labels condition meta-training.

evaluations.setting: Original held-out-trajectory nearest-neighbor test over all five G.pt models
evaluations.metric: Fraction of generated samples closer to one of 200 checkpoints on the input-linked test run than to any training checkpoint
evaluations.result: Cartpole and CIFAR-10 score 100% for all prompts; MNIST is 100% for most prompts but falls to roughly 15-20% at the smallest prompts.
evaluations.baseline: Millions of raw training checkpoints, without symmetry alignment, interpolation/noise baselines, or comparison to ordinary between-run distances.

limitations: Each G.pt model is restricted to one fixed architecture, task, and conditioning metric.
Target models are tiny MLPs or CNNs with 1,250-7,960 parameters, while G.pt models contain 347M-639M parameters in Table 1 and scaling reaches 858M.
Every inference sample requires 1,000 transformer forward passes under the released DDPM sampler.
One-step baselines are not compute-, time-, memory-, energy-, or data-cost matched.
The 23M-checkpoint, 425GB extracted corpus requires more than 100K prior training runs and creates a large unreported amortization burden.
No total pre-training or data-generation compute, hardware type, wall time, energy, or carbon estimate is reported, despite the appendix checklist answering yes to the compute question.
Supervised models use canonical benchmark test labels repeatedly to calculate conditioning targets for every checkpoint.
CIFAR-10.1 is a shifted diagnostic, not a replacement iid test set for label-leakage-free evaluation.
Dataset trajectories use static optimizer hyperparameters and limited architectures, datasets, and objectives.
Same-run pairing favors imitation of the optimizers and training schedules that generated the corpus.
The method struggles to extrapolate outside its prompt distribution and underfits the CIFAR-10 metric landscape.
Prompt values used for headline one-step results can be moved above or below the best corpus value when that empirically performs better.
Scaling plots select the checkpoint with the best prompt alignment observed over training, but a separate model-selection split is not described.
The headline optimizer bars use only five input initializations.
Prompt alignment compresses heterogeneous desired-versus-observed curves into mean R-squared and can be negative or dominated by prompt-range choice.
Out-of-distribution evidence changes only the initialization distribution for the same MNIST architecture and task.
The local PCA plots use sample-fitted directions and filter out samples with two-dimensional reconstruction error at or above 10^-3.
Parameter variation does not imply distinct functions, basins, or useful ensemble diversity.
The original nearest-neighbor score is tied to the conditioning trajectory and is not a valid exclusion of copying or interpolation.
A later dedicated primary audit finds strong copying in the original 2.1M-checkpoint G.pt setting.
Permutation augmentation does not make the transformer invariant or equivariant to parameter symmetries and omits scaling and other function-preserving transformations.
The public code has no tests, CI, pinned artifact hashes, or scripts for several central paper figures and ablations.
The released data and model downloads remain online but are approximately 349GB compressed and 32.3GB respectively, limiting practical verification.
failure_modes: A requested loss or error outside the checkpoint support yields biased, saturated, or nonsensical parameters.
A new architecture changes token identities and dimensions, making a trained G.pt unusable without a separate model.
A new dataset or objective breaks the learned trajectory prior even when the target network architecture is unchanged.
The generated network copies or interpolates a nearby stored solution while passing raw held-out-trajectory checks.
Unmodeled permutation, sign, or scaling symmetries make Euclidean proximity and density artificially multimodal.
A low target prompt chosen outside the reachable region produces worse performance than a slightly less ambitious prompt.
Repeated recursive prompting drifts away from the trajectory distribution used in same-run pair training.
Conditioning on a benchmark test metric learns idiosyncrasies of that fixed test set and inflates reported test performance.
A favorable single-update count hides inference that is slower or more expensive than many conventional gradient updates.
A high average prompt-alignment score masks poor individual networks, prompt regions, or tail failures.
PCA projection merges distant modes or fabricates apparent basins, and reconstruction filtering suppresses contrary samples.
Parameter augmentation improves held-out fit without teaching the model an invariant representation of weight space.
Downloader corruption or supply-chain changes go undetected because large artifacts have no published cryptographic hashes.
The Python 3.8, PyTorch 1.11, CUDA 11.3, and manually installed IsaacGym stack becomes difficult to reproduce on current systems.
reusable_insights: Treat optimizer update count, model evaluations, wall time, FLOPs, memory, and amortized meta-training cost as separate axes.
Use untouched validation and test splits for conditioning, prompt selection, checkpoint selection, and final reporting.
Compare trajectory-conditioned generators with simple regressors, nearest-trajectory retrieval, weight interpolation, and noise-addition baselines.
Measure novelty after exact or approximate symmetry alignment and in function space, not only raw Euclidean parameter space.
A conditioning-linked held-out trajectory can test trajectory prediction but cannot by itself exclude training-set copying.
Store dense intermediate checkpoints when learning training dynamics, but ablate unique runs separately from checkpoints per run.
Encode weight symmetries in the architecture or canonicalization procedure instead of relying only on augmentation.
Report the full desired-versus-observed curve and per-instance distribution alongside aggregate R-squared.
Distinguish stochastic variation, basin diversity, behavioral diversity, ensemble benefit, and genuine distribution coverage.
Evaluate cross-task, cross-data, cross-architecture, cross-optimizer, and horizon shift independently.
Publish immutable hashes, exact figure scripts, hardware and compute logs, and small deterministic smoke tests for very large artifacts.
Audit later independent evidence: the CVPR 2026 copying analysis materially changes how the original Appendix E result should be interpreted.
open_questions: Can a checkpoint generator beat compute-matched tuned optimizers after including all 1,000 denoising evaluations and amortized corpus cost?
Can consistency, flow-matching, or autoregressive samplers preserve prompt control with one or a few network evaluations?
What invariant or equivariant representation scales across width, depth, layer type, architecture, and parameter symmetry?
How much performance comes from conditional retrieval or interpolation versus learned reusable optimization structure?
Can training on many tasks, objectives, architectures, and optimizer schedules yield genuine meta-generalization?
Does weight generation remain beneficial when conditioning metrics use validation data and final evaluation uses untouched labels?
Which behavioral and symmetry-aligned metrics reliably separate memorization, interpolation, and novel useful solutions?
Why does data scaling from 2.1M to 20.4M checkpoints reduce G.pt copying, and is unique-run diversity more important than checkpoint count?
Can a generated population improve ensemble accuracy or uncertainty after matching accuracy, compute, and distance to training models?
How stable is recursive prompting far beyond the same-run horizons seen during training?
Can training-data generation and inference be made economical enough for target networks that are not orders of magnitude smaller than the generator?
Would architecture-native graph representations outperform per-position encoders and decoders while retaining conditional metric control?

competitive_landscape.title: Hyper-Representations as Generative Models: Sampling Unseen Neural Network Weights
competitive_landscape.relationship: Near-contemporaneous model-zoo generator that learns an autoencoded weight representation and samples unseen weights.
competitive_landscape.difference: Hyper-Representations samples from a task-agnostic latent space and evaluates initialization, ensembles, and transfer after fine-tuning; G.pt conditions a much larger diffusion transformer on a starting checkpoint and desired metric to directly predict a later same-task checkpoint.
competitive_landscape.source_version: current arXiv abstract and full-text record checked 2026-08-24

competitive_landscape.title: VeLO: Training Versatile Learned Optimizers by Scaling Up
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct learned-optimizer alternative targeting general-purpose optimization across a wide task distribution.
competitive_landscape.difference: VeLO ingests gradients and emits iterative updates with one reusable optimizer across tasks, whereas G.pt generates a whole future checkpoint with 1,000 denoising evaluations and requires one model per task, architecture, and metric.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Network Diffusion
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later latent-diffusion competitor for synthesizing high-performing neural-network parameters.
competitive_landscape.difference: P-diff autoencodes and unconditionally diffuses full small networks or selected parameter subsets from high-performing checkpoints; G.pt directly diffuses all parameters and conditions on an input network plus requested metric, but is much more tightly bound to a single trajectory distribution.
competitive_landscape.source_version: current arXiv v3 full-text record checked 2026-08-24

competitive_landscape.title: $\mu$LO: Compute-Efficient Meta-Generalization of Learned Optimizers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Compute-conscious learned optimizer emphasizing width, depth, and horizon generalization.
competitive_landscape.difference: $\mu$LO applies maximal-update parameterization to gradient-based learned optimizers and reports training below 250 GPU-hours with transfer to substantially wider, deeper, and longer-horizon tasks; G.pt reports no compute budget and demonstrates only initialization-distribution shift within one architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: Recurrent Diffusion for Large-Scale Parameter Generation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later diffusion competitor designed to generate complete parameters for modern large architectures.
competitive_landscape.difference: RPG recurrently models relationships between parameter tokens and scales generation to hundreds of millions of target parameters across ResNet, ConvNeXt, ViT, COCO, ImageNet, and LoRA settings; G.pt's largest target network has 7,960 parameters and architecture-specific token maps.

competitive_landscape.title: Generative Modeling of Weights: Generalization or Memorization?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Dedicated independent primary audit of G.pt and three other prominent weight generators, published as a CVPR 2026 Highlight.
competitive_landscape.difference: Zeng et al. add symmetry-aware weight-space distances, behavior similarity, copying tests, and interpolation/noise baselines; they find substantial memorization in the original G.pt setting and show that expanding its data from 2.1M to 20.4M checkpoints mitigates it, directly revising the interpretation of G.pt Appendix E.
competitive_landscape.source_version: current arXiv full text and CVPR 2026 accepted version checked 2026-08-24

competitive_landscape.title: DeepWeightFlow: Re-Basined Flow Matching for Generating Neural Network Weights
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current ICLR 2026 competitor for efficient complete weight generation.
competitive_landscape.difference: DeepWeightFlow uses flow matching plus Git Re-Basin or TransFusion canonicalization, generates complete MLP, ResNet, ViT, and BERT weights without fine-tuning, and emphasizes minutes-scale population sampling; G.pt uses augmentation rather than canonicalization, 1,000-step diffusion, and tiny fixed target architectures.
competitive_landscape.source_version: current arXiv v2 and ICLR 2026 record checked 2026-08-24

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a scalable data-driven route to learned optimization: a conditional diffusion transformer trained directly on checkpoint trajectories can optimize unseen initial parameters in one update, follow metric prompts, handle nondifferentiable objectives, generate multimodal solutions, generalize to new initialization distributions, and improve predictably with model and data scale.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Using dense checkpoint trajectories as a generative pre-training corpus and conditioning directly on a desired future metric was genuinely original and helped establish weight space as a data modality. The strongest optimizer framing is not supported: one update means 1,000 large-transformer evaluations, test labels supervise the classification models, tasks and architectures are fixed, and no compute-matched comparison exists. More importantly, the paper's own nearest-neighbor diagnostic is structurally weak, and the later CVPR 2026 audit finds substantial copying in the exact original G.pt regime. The work remains an influential proof of concept for trajectory-conditioned weight generation, but not evidence of an efficient, general, or clearly non-memorizing learned optimizer.

reviewer_notes: Audited the exact sole arXiv v1 PDF (18/18 pages), fresh e-print source, all equations, both algorithms, Tables 1-2, Figures 1-14, appendices A-E, and checklist. The fresh v1 PDF byte-matched the pinned cache at SHA-256 694dd0549b0e76dda4f7ee561fb95edf51369bfb63c82b2671e1ad10318bd8c4; source archive SHA-256 was 3a4909b09184fa7ca85d4f33ee1a16d69889abdc079197548b89ccff1560086e. Inspected official artifact HEAD fd072255a5ad33990b88ffcbef462e1b31fb6d96 (five commits; last 2022-10-03), README, environment, download routes, data loaders, augmentation, task metrics, transformer, sampler, configs, training loop, and visualization code. All five model URLs and three dataset URLs were range-accessible on 2026-08-24; reported Content-Length totals were 32,321,551,253 and 348,849,305,036 bytes respectively. Static compilation passed, but the repository has no tests, CI, artifact checksums, or scripts for several paper-only experiments, and full numerical reproduction was infeasible without downloading roughly 381GB of archives and recreating the unreported original compute environment. Current primary competitors and the later dedicated copying audit were checked through 2026-08-24.
